title: Stacks & Queues
relevance: Stacks and queues are core interview primitives for modeling LIFO/FIFO behavior, monotonic next-greater patterns, and O(1) cache designs in OAs and SDE rounds.

phases.goal: Establish LIFO vs FIFO, constant-time core ops, and how C++ adapters sit on an underlying container.

must_hit.point: A stack is LIFO and a queue is FIFO.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States last-in-first-out for stacks and first-in-first-out for queues.

must_hit.point: Both structures offer core push/pop-style operations in O(1) time.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names push/pop (or enqueue/dequeue) and cites O(1) for the core ops.

must_hit.point: In C++, std::stack and std::queue are container adapters that wrap an underlying container, by default std::deque.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions adapters (not owning memory themselves) and default deque.

must_hit.point: A std::deque allows fast insertion and deletion at both its beginning and its end.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Defines deque as double-ended with fast ops at both ends.

probes: What is the difference between a stack and a queue, and what are their core operation complexities?
In C++, what are std::stack and std::queue, and what underlying container do they use by default?

hints.1: Think about order of removal: which end do you take from?
hints.2: Contrast LIFO with FIFO, then mention O(1) push/pop and C++ adapters over a sequence container.
hints.3: Stack = LIFO, queue = FIFO, core ops O(1); std::stack/std::queue are adapters wrapping std::deque by default.

phases.goal: Show how stacks/queues are implemented and how classic stack algorithms (parens, min stack, expressions, monotonic order) actually run.

must_hit.point: Array stack: keep a topIndex starting at -1; push increments then stores, pop decrements—all O(1).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes topIndex = -1 and ++/-- index updates without shifting.

must_hit.point: Array queue: use front and rear with circular indexing and a size counter so enqueue/dequeue stay O(1) instead of shifting left in O(n).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions circular rear/front updates and that naive front-shift pop is O(n).

must_hit.point: Stack via one queue: on push, enqueue then rotate prior elements so the new element sits at the front; push is O(n), pop/top are O(1).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Explains cycling n existing elements after push so LIFO pop works from the queue front.

must_hit.point: Queue via two stacks: always push to input; when output is empty, transfer all input→output so FIFO pops are amortized O(1) (each element moves once).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names input/output stacks and amortized O(1) because transfer only when output is empty.

must_hit.point: Linked-list stack uses head as top (O(1) insert/delete at head); linked-list queue needs head and tail, and must set tail to nullptr when the last node is popped.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Head-as-top for stack; head+tail for queue with empty-tail edge case.

must_hit.point: Valid parentheses: push opens; a close must match stack top then pop; final stack empty means valid—nested brackets mirror LIFO.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Walks push-open / match-and-pop-close / empty-at-end, and ties nesting to LIFO.

must_hit.point: Min stack encoding: on new min x, push 2x - minElement as a flag and set minElement = x; on pop of a flagged value (< minElement), restore prior min via 2×minElement - popped.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Gives the 2x - prev_min flag and the restore formula; notes long long for overflow.

must_hit.point: Monotonic stack keeps strictly increasing or decreasing order by popping violators; each element is pushed and popped at most once, so next-greater/smaller scans are O(n).
must_hit.evidence_hint: States maintain order by popping, and O(n) because each element enters/leaves once.

probes: How would you implement a queue with an array without making pop O(n)?
How do you implement a queue using two stacks with amortized O(1) pop?
How can getMin on a stack be O(1) without storing a (value, min) pair on every push?

hints.1: For the array queue, avoid shifting every element on dequeue.
hints.2: Use circular front/rear (plus size), or two stacks with lazy transfer when the output stack is empty; for min, encode a sentinel below the new min.
hints.3: Circular queue: rear = (rear+1)%capacity; two-stack queue: transfer input→output only when output empty (amortized O(1)); min stack: push 2x-oldMin when x is new min, restore with 2*min-top on pop.

phases.goal: Compare competing implementations and algorithms on time, space, and when each pattern wins.

must_hit.point: Fixed array stack/queue: O(1) ops and O(n) capacity space, but overflow at capacity; linked list versions are dynamic O(n) nodes with pointer overhead.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Contrasts fixed capacity overflow vs dynamic nodes and constant pointer overhead.

must_hit.point: Stack-from-queue pays O(n) on push to keep pop O(1); queue-from-stacks keeps push O(1) and makes pop/peek amortized O(1) (worst-case O(n) on transfer).
must_hit.evidence_hint: States which op is expensive in each simulation and mentions amortized vs worst-case.

must_hit.point: Min stack: pairs (value, current_min) are simpler extra space; encoding with one minElement uses one value per push and still O(1) ops.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Compares pair-per-entry vs encoded single-value approach.

must_hit.point: Trapping rain water: brute left/right max per bar is O(n^2); precomputed max arrays are O(n) time and O(n) space; two-pointers achieve O(n) time and O(1) space; a monotonic stack computes basins horizontally.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Lists brute vs precompute vs two-pointer space and mentions stack horizontal approach.

must_hit.point: Sliding window maximum: brute O(n × k), heap O(n log n), monotonic deque O(n) by evicting out-of-window fronts and dominated backs.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names the three complexities and that deque stores indices in decreasing order.

must_hit.point: LRU needs hash map + doubly linked list for O(1) get/put with arbitrary eviction; LFU needs key→node plus frequency→list buckets (and min_freq) for O(1) frequency-and-recency eviction—heap LFU is O(log n).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Contrasts map+DLL for LRU vs nested freq lists for LFU, and rejects heap as too slow.

probes: When would you prefer an array-backed queue over a linked-list queue?
Compare implementing a stack with a queue versus a queue with two stacks—where does the cost land?
For sliding window maximum, why is a monotonic deque preferable to a heap?

hints.1: Look at capacity limits, which operation you make expensive, and extra space for mins or windows.
hints.2: Array = fixed capacity O(1); linked list = growable; simulation cost sits on push or on amortized transfer; window max: deque beats heap’s log factor.
hints.3: Array overflows at capacity but O(1); list grows with pointer overhead; stack←queue makes push O(n); queue←stacks amortizes pop; deque gives O(n) window max vs O(n log n) heap.

phases.goal: Apply stacks, monotonic stacks/deques, and map+list designs to standard interview problems.

must_hit.point: Next Greater Element: right-to-left monotonic decreasing stack; map answers for a subset in O(N + M); circular NGE II simulates 2n indices with i % n.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes decreasing stack from the right, hashmap for nums1, and 2n unroll for circular.

must_hit.point: Water above bar i is min(left_max, right_max) - height[i]; two pointers move the side with the smaller max.
must_hit.evidence_hint: States the min-of-bounds formula and moving the smaller-max pointer.

must_hit.point: Sum of subarray minimums uses contribution: with PSE at L and NSE at R, arr[i] is strict min in (i-L)*(R-i) subarrays; use strict < on one side and <= on the other to avoid duplicate overcount; answer modulo 10^9 + 7.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Gives (i-L)*(R-i), asymmetric < / <= for duplicates, and mod 10^9+7.

must_hit.point: Largest rectangle in histogram: for each bar, width extends to nearest smaller left/right; single-pass increasing stack computes area when a smaller bar becomes NSE-right.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Explains NSE bounds and popping to compute height*width in one pass.

must_hit.point: Maximal rectangle: per row, heights count consecutive 1s above; run histogram largest-rectangle each row in O(R × C).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Treats each row as histogram base and cites O(R × C).

must_hit.point: Remove k digits: greedy monotonic increasing digit stack—pop larger previous digits while k > 0, then strip leading zeros.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Smaller digit in a higher place wins; pop while k remains.

must_hit.point: Stock span equals distance to previous greater; stack of {price, span} gives O(1) amortized per next.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Pops <= prices accumulating spans, then +1 for today.

must_hit.point: Celebrity: knows(a,b) eliminates one candidate; two pointers find a candidate in n - 1 queries, then verify with a full pass (about 2n more knows calls).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Elimination then verify; cites n-1 then verification calls.

must_hit.point: LRU: unordered_map key→node plus DLL (MRU at head, LRU at tail), dummy head/tail; LFU: key_table plus freq_table lists and min_freq, ties broken by LRU within the min frequency list.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Map+DLL move-to-front for LRU; freq buckets + min_freq and tail eviction for LFU.

probes: How do you find the next greater element for every index in O(n)?
Explain how to compute trapped rain water in O(1) extra space.
Design an LRU cache with O(1) get and put—what structures do you need?

hints.1: For next-greater and spans, think about what you can safely discard from a stack.
hints.2: Monotonic decreasing stack from the right for NGE; for water, two pointers on the smaller boundary; for LRU, map to nodes in a doubly linked list.
hints.3: NGE: pop <= while scanning right-to-left; water: add left_max-height[left] when left side is the bottleneck; LRU: hash map + DLL with move-to-head and evict tail.

tradeoffs.strong_answer: Arrays give O(1) ops with O(n) fixed capacity and overflow risk; linked lists grow dynamically with O(n) node allocations and pointer overhead, using head (stack) or head+tail (queue) for O(1) ends.

tradeoffs.topic: Stack using a queue vs queue using two stacks
tradeoffs.strong_answer: One-queue stack rotates on push so push is O(n) and pop/top are O(1). Two-stack queue pushes to input in O(1) and transfers to output only when empty, making pop/peek amortized O(1) though a single transfer is O(n).

tradeoffs.topic: Min stack pairs vs encoded minElement
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Storing (value, current_min) pairs is simple and O(1) per op with extra space per entry; encoding 2x - oldMin when x is a new min uses one stack value per push and restores the prior min on pop, still O(1), with care for overflow via long long.

tradeoffs.topic: Trapping rain water: precompute vs two pointers vs stack
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Precomputed left/right max arrays are O(n) time and O(n) space; two pointers track left_max/right_max and move the smaller side for O(n) time and O(1) space; a monotonic decreasing stack fills water horizontally by basin when a taller bar appears.

tradeoffs.topic: Sliding window maximum: brute vs heap vs monotonic deque
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Brute rescans each window in O(n × k); a max-heap is O(n log n) but must handle expired indices; a decreasing deque of indices evicts out-of-window fronts and dominated backs for O(n) time and O(k) space.

LRU pairs a hash map with a doubly linked list so access moves a node to MRU and eviction pops the tail in O(1). LFU groups nodes into frequency lists (map key→node, map freq→list) plus min_freq so eviction is O(1); a frequency heap would be O(log n) and is too slow for the O(1) requirement.

gotchas.trap: Implementing an array queue by popping from index 0 and shifting the rest left.
gotchas.correction: That makes pop O(n). Use circular front/rear indices (and a size counter) so enqueue and dequeue stay O(1).

gotchas.trap: Assuming every pop/peek on a two-stack queue is strictly O(1) in the worst case.
gotchas.correction: Transferring input→output is O(n) when output is empty, but each element moves to output once and is popped once, so amortized cost is O(1).

gotchas.trap: Forgetting to clear tail when a linked-list queue’s last element is popped.
gotchas.correction: When head becomes nullptr after pop, also set tail to nullptr so the next push treats the queue as empty.

gotchas.trap: Treating ^ like left-associative operators in infix→postfix.
gotchas.correction: Precedence still pops >= for left-associative ops, but for ^ do not pop another ^ (right-associative); prefix conversion flips the precedence/associativity handling after reversing.

gotchas.trap: On min-stack pop/top, treating an encoded flag as a real value.
gotchas.correction: If topVal < minElement, top should return minElement, and pop should restore minElement = 2*minElement - topVal.

gotchas.trap: Counting duplicate minima twice in sum of subarray minimums.
gotchas.correction: Use strict NSE on one side and previous smaller-or-equal on the other (strict < vs <=) so each equal element owns a disjoint set of subarrays.

gotchas.trap: Using only a hash map (or only a queue) for LRU.
gotchas.correction: A map gives O(1) lookup but not O(1) recency updates/eviction; a queue cannot remove an arbitrary middle key in O(1). Combine unordered_map with a doubly linked list (dummy head/tail help).

gotchas.trap: Picking the wrong structure for the problem family.
gotchas.correction: Matching/nesting → stack; sliding-window extremes → monotonic deque; next greater/smaller → monotonic stack; LRU/LFU → hash map plus linked list (freq buckets for LFU).
